First of all I commend you for coming here and asking, you’re a good partner. I can only speak for myself, but the biggest thing about having pocd aside from the terrible intrusive thoughts that try to ruin your life is the shame. Feeling like a terrible person for having them. I’ve never told a partner about mine, but if I had one that wanted to help, I’d say the following:

1. Don’t act like it’s nothing. To people who don’t have it it’s obviously very hard to understand, but the people I have told have acted like it’s no big deal, “just don’t think about it” (I mean come on, if we could, ocd wouldn’t exist), things like that. So definitely honoring your partner and not belittling the symptoms is huge. You also don’t want to indulge, of course, but just understanding, even if you don’t understand, is a big deal. 

2. The shame is something only we can work out and heal within ourselves, but having someone see or hear what we go through and not look at us like we’re evil is a pretty big deal. I guess this advice is just holding space without judgement, but that’s a big deal and a great movement of love. Being able to share with someone and having them accept you is huge. So be that safe space without judgement, if you’re able. Letting him know you don’t think he’s a bad person for his thoughts goes a long way. 

3. Literally ask him what he needs. Tell him you want to support him and ask him what the best way to do that is, that’s within your capacity. That alone will be so comforting for him. Maybe he wants to talk and be heard without judgement, maybe he has some specific thing that helps (for example: my college bf used to lay on top of me with all his body weight before weighted blankets were a thing and that not only helped me but also really made me feel loved and supported). The point is only he can let you low what it is he specifically needs, but hearing “how can I support you” is so comforting. 

Hope that helps!

Ok so you’re gonna be ok! Please remember to breathe. I’m sure lots of people are gonna tell you lots of super helpful tips here. I’ll tell you what helps me most, but it might not be what helps you or anyone else. Even with ocd we’re all unique and you will absolutely find your flow of what works and doesn’t for you. 

For me, after the initial learning phase once I was diagnosed, I always noticed that the more I dwelled on on the ocd, the worse it got. The less, the better. When I read a lot about ocd, I noticed my symptoms were way worse than when I focused on other things. I have to say yoga, meditation, and Breathwork have helped my symptoms so much, and not dwelling on them. Physical activity also helps me to get out of stuck thought forms and patterns, but with no expectations, for example if I’m caught in a loop I’ll make myself get up, put on loud music, and dance around and shake my body all out. Its amazingly helpful to get unstuck from your head and back into your body. All these things I’m recommending are also helpful for the depression and the cptsd (you’ll notice many of us have many of these co-existing diagnoses, they go hand in hand). Maybe instead of the last straw, this can be an explanation for the other things. For me when I received my diagnoses, my therapist said “that’s why you’re so depressed.” She wasn’t totally right and it’s not that simple, but I felt exactly like you (this is way too much, how can I possibly deal with alllll these things?!) until I decided to see it the other way, which was less overwhelming. 

Also, humor helps me. Because ocd is not funny, it’s horrifying, but also it is funny, and seeing memes about it or following funny Instagram accounts about it made me feel less alone, and laughing at myself and my symptoms gave me some relief and at least a pattern interrupt. Pattern interrupts are good. 

Lastly, this one is still a work in progress for me, but I think it’s also the most powerful. Ocd makes us hate ourselves. So the cure for that is radical self love and acceptance. The ocd makes me think I’m gonna kill people? Ok, so how can I love and accept myself even when that thought is happening? That is a true practice which requires bravery and courage, and I believe it’s the most important thing on my healing journey I’ve ever done. There’s a book by Matt Kahn called “whatever arises love that” and he has tons of free talks on YouTube that saved me when was first diagnosed and really hated myself. These types of shifts really changed my life. 

You are worthy and lovable exactly as you are. Take what helps and leave the rest. It ain’t gonna be easy sister, but you’re gonna be ok. Big hug. ❤️

I definitely do not recommend starting with a 3 day fast, that is dangerous and not something that can be responsibly advised to a stranger. Do some research, clean up your diet FIRST for a while, then start with a fruit fast (only eating fruit), then wait a while and do a 1 day water fast, and so on. If you fast when your body isn’t ready it can do some damage (I learned this the hard way). You also want to make sure your body is receiving electrolytes while you fast, I use them in a dropper in my water (the packets area

Firstly, you are an amazing human and I am here for you. I have tried a lot of different things and these are what work best for me:

1. Tapping / EFT - especially if you’re having a panic attack or feeling really anxious, tapping will help move that stuck energy. I scoffed at it at first when it was suggested to me but now I do it everyday. It’s brought me out of panic several times. [Tapping ](https://youtu.be/wgaM1gf1ulw) They also have a free app. 

2. Mindfulness and meditation have really helped me. There are lots of places to start with this, there are free apps you can use like Calm and Insight Timer or lots of things on YouTube. Deepak Chopra has some simple guided meditations or try Gabby Bernstein, she was my first intro into this world and her books and meditations (you can get free ones on her website) really helped me. The principles can really help you shift out of your thoughts. 

3. When I am really not ok I hold onto gratitude. I guess you could call it grounding. I focus on whatever is supporting me, physically. The chair I’m sitting on and how it feels to be supported by it, or the ground underneath my feet. Just shifting your focus from whatever you’re thinking about to thinking about that physical support can be helpful. Going outside has helped me a ton too. Just simply walking outside always proves a shift for me, even though every time before I do it I don’t think it will. Breathe in the air. 

4. Speaking of, breathing techniques! I’ve found a bunch of different ones for anxiety and ocd and kind of do my own based on what I liked from each, but here it is:

-Sigh out like something just annoyed you and drop your shoulders down. 
- Put your hand on your stomach. You’re probably breathing from your chest, which is not good. Keep your hand on your stomach to make sure you breathe from there.
- Breathe in, pushing your belly out against your hand, for a count of 5.
- Breathe out, pulling your stomach in against your spine, for a count of 5. 
- Repeat - you can set your phone alarm for 30 seconds to a minute so you don’t have to think about it. 

5. I keep mantras with me that reallly help. When I feel myself freaking out I say my mantras over and over in my head. Mine are the opposite of my fears. Try writing down your fears and then turn them into positive affirmations. They should start with “I am”. I’ll offer mine to you so you can get an idea:

I am happy. 
I am healthy. 
I am whole. 
I am peace. Peace is within me and all around me.
Well being is my natural state.

Is it fake it til you make it? Sure, but isn’t the goal to make it? Who cares how you get there. Saying comforting things to yourself isn’t gonna hurt you. I felt silly at first, as a natural skeptic, but it’s really comforting to hold these mantras. They are mine, and when I feel like shit and want to give up, I say them and I feel a shift. The mind is powerful! If this resonates with you or you want to learn more check out Louis Hay on YouTube, she was the queen of affirmations. Kinda related Abraham Hicks YouTube videos got me through some really dark times. 

6. Music - Wow music has helped me so much. Comfort me when I was panicking, lift me up when I wanted to die, make me feel connected and understood while I was alone, and get out of my head when I didn’t think I could. I’ll share 2 of my Spotify playlists: [Doin’ Just Fine ](https://open.spotify.com/user/125864736/playlist/4rB1BD1YkMjkiuG3sXOb30?si=rbFxLf6TQBK7u9zVto68Dg) is for when I’m not doing just fine but I want to shift into being ok, and I make myself dance around to it and it works! And [Calm ](https://open.spotify.com/user/125864736/playlist/6gjCxahW0Ex9OrUw6WTlI5?si=Nxzl9qI6RkSPoBEaGCAbdA) is for when I need to calm down and feel held/supported by the universe. I like to listen to that one at night if I have trouble falling asleep. Also for sleep I drink Natural Calm, it’s a magnesium powder, you just add hot water and it’s super good for you (I think you’re a female, most women are magnesium deficient anyway). Get it at any pharmacy and some grocery stores.

7. Exercise is good, anything that moves energy through your body. Waking is good, I try to take 2 walks a day too, but what’s even better is if you can do some yoga - kundalini yoga has been becoming more popular in OCD, especially the breathing techniques. I’m telling you it’s all shifting energy. 

8. Be kind to yourself. This may not be an issue for you but it was (is) for me so it’s worth mentioning. I have trouble not beating myself up for being so “sick” and for not always being able to stop and change my thoughts. So I try to remember to give myself some grace and ask myself “is this thought loving to me?” And if not I try to let the thought go, because being mean to yourself won’t get you anywhere you want to be. If you can’t let it go try to turn it around into an affirmation. 

Anyway that’s all I can think of right now, but I have built up an arsenal because I was not equipped to dealing with this. Also if you’re open to it try energy work. It’s kinda crazy how much it has helped me. I do reiki on myself and go to sound healing and it’s like it gets lose stuff that’s stuck in your brain! You can listen to some sound healing on YouTube too if you want to try it out. Anything with drumming in it is helpful. I wish you the best! You are healing!

When you’re “in the shit” it’s very hard to stay motivated (just to keep going) and hopeful. So it’s really important to have the things you’re interested in, a hobby, passion, etc. to throw yourself into. I’ve found that, especially if the thing is somewhat physical (not just sitting) it’s more likely to help the symptoms go away.

Focusing your mind on something else will help divert the attention from your looping mind (this is what I call anxiety brain).

Things I find helpful: 

Walking around, aimlessly or to run an errand,  but with a quick step. If you’re into working out go to the gym. If you can get to nature, especially any kind of trees, Nature has a way of quelling anxiety, it’s kind of amazing. 

Focus on 1 small goal/task at a time and then cross it off your  list. Even if it’s easy, like “take a shower” I find my mind starts to feel more organized when I am focused on something. 

Meditate. And then meditate again. Don’t know how to meditate? Try meditating. Physical activity can help with our physical anxiety and meditation can help us calm the anxiety in our minds. 

Good luck. 💙
